planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in a chunky, well-drained aroid mix; a stabilized, patented selection named for Philippine president Corazon Aquino.

directions: This clumping aroid produces deeply heart-shaped, matte leaves marked by stark white to pale-silver veins radiating from a dark, upright petiole. Keep it warm and humid year-round, and let the top inch of the chunky mix dry between waterings to avoid rhizome rot. Divide offsets from the rhizome once a clump has three or more mature leaves to propagate true-to-type plants. Protect from cold drafts and direct midday sun, which will scorch the matte foliage.

common_name: Metallic Blue Alocasia (Iridescent Heterophylla Elephant Ear)

planting.note: Best grown as a small houseplant in bright, indirect light in a chunky, fast-draining aroid mix; a compact Philippine species selection under 20 inches tall.

directions: This diminutive selection of Alocasia heterophylla carries corrugated, narrow-triangular leaves with a distinctive iridescent blue-grey sheen that shifts with the light. Its small stature and 3-5 leaf rosette make it well suited to terrariums or tight shelf space rather than floor displays. Provide high humidity and bright but filtered light to preserve the metallic leaf cast, since low light dulls the sheen to flat green. Repot only when clearly rootbound, since this species resents excessive root disturbance.

common_name: Ninja Alocasia (Black Velvet Sport with Crisp Double Veining)

planting.note: Grow as a small tabletop houseplant in bright, indirect light in a chunky, well-drained aroid mix; a darker, more sharply veined sport of 'Black Velvet'.

directions: This dwarf sport of Alocasia reginula carries thick, near-black velvet leaves traced with crisp, pale double veins that stand out more sharply than on the standard Black Velvet form. It stays under 14 inches tall, making it well suited to small pots on a bright windowsill or under grow lights. Let the chunky mix dry out fully between waterings, since this rhizomatous species is highly prone to rot in soggy conditions. Divide offsets from the base once a clump is established to increase your collection true to type.

common_name: Morocco Alocasia (Glossy White-Veined Hybrid with Burgundy Leaf Backs)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, filtered light in a rich, well-drained mix; a vigorous Florida-bred hybrid of 'Aurora' and 'Polly'.

directions: Discovered among greenhouse seedlings from a controlled cross of 'Aurora' and 'Polly', this hybrid produces glossy green, arrow-shaped leaves etched with bright white veins and backed in deep burgundy, carried on pale pink petioles. Strong basal offshoots quickly build a dense, symmetrical clump, giving faster bulk than many slower Alocasia hybrids. Keep the soil evenly moist but never waterlogged, since standing water quickly leads to rhizome rot. Give it more filtered brightness than typical shade aroids to keep the vein contrast crisp and the growth compact.

common_name: Nancy's Revenge Elephant Ear (Yellow-Veined Chartreuse Taro)

planting.note: Plant tubers in rich, moisture-retentive soil in sun to part shade after the soil has warmed; a Caribbean-collected heirloom introduced through the aroid society circuit in 2000.

directions: Leaves emerge solid light green, then develop a bold, buttercream-yellow blaze that pours down the central vein and branches into the side veins once the plant begins to flower, since the coloring is genetically linked to bloom onset. Vigorous stoloniferous growth sends out runners that root readily in consistently moist, rich soil, so give it room to spread or grow it in a large submerged container to contain it. It tolerates more sun than most shade aroids provided the soil stays evenly wet, and it dies back to a hardy rhizome after frost in marginal zones. Mulch heavily over winter where grown at the cold edge of its range to protect the crown.

common_name: Kona Coffee Elephant Ear (Compact Coffee-Brown Royal Hawaiian Taro)

planting.note: Plant tubers in rich, evenly moist soil in full sun to part shade after the soil has warmed; a 2011 Dr. John Cho introduction and the first dwarf member of the Royal Hawaiian series.

directions: New leaves emerge an almost fluorescent green before quickly deepening to a rich coffee-brown with purple-black undertones and a glossy sheen. Its dwarf, tightly clumping habit tops out around three feet, making it far more container- and border-friendly than the giant black-leaved taro cultivars. Unlike many shade-loving Colocasia, it colors up best and stays compact with several hours of direct sun alongside consistently moist, fertile soil. It shows above-average cold tolerance for the genus, often persisting as a perennial well north of typical taro hardiness limits with a heavy winter mulch.

common_name: White Lava Elephant Ear (Glossy Green Taro with Bold White Veins)

planting.note: Plant tubers in rich, moisture-retentive soil in partial shade after the soil has warmed; a patented Hawaii breeding-program selection with a glossy 'Black Lava' counterpart.

directions: This seedling selection from a controlled Hawaiian breeding program pairs medium-glossy green leaves with flamboyant white veining and lightly undulating margins, carried on glossy red petioles. It reads as a bright, variegated-looking counterpart to the same breeder's dark 'Black Lava' cultivar, giving strong color contrast in mixed tropical plantings. Give it steady moisture and rich soil, since the large leaves wilt quickly if the root zone dries out. Divide congested clumps every couple of years in spring to maintain vigorous new growth and strong vein contrast.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in a rich, well-drained mix; needs strong light to hold its bold white venation.

directions: This tuberous South American aroid produces rich green, heart-shaped leaves accentuated by thick, chalk-white veins radiating along the midrib and margins, more pronounced than on the straight species. It needs consistently bright, indirect light to keep the white venation crisp, since lower light causes the contrast to fade toward plain green. Water when the top inch of soil dries out, and reduce watering if the rhizome goes dormant in cooler, drier conditions. Because the whole plant is toxic if ingested, site it away from pets and small children.
